title: It's the message that matters
grammar: Cleft sentences (It is… that… / What… is…)

scene.speaker: nova
scene.bubble: This unit is all about emphasis. Learn cleft sentences — It is… that…, What… is… — and put the spotlight exactly where you want it.
scene.intro: Welcome back. Some of the most powerful sentences in English do one simple thing: they place a single idea in the spotlight. In this unit our club studies rhetoric and emphasis — from Melville's Ahab to the great speeches of history — and you learn the cleft sentence, the elegant structure that lets you say, quite literally, ‘It is this that matters.’ You will also tackle key word transformations from the exam. For the Inspiring Nordic project, this is the grammar of persuasion. Let's begin.

activities.title: Reading — the reading club on rhetoric

data.title: It's the message that matters
data.author: liam
data.text:
What separates a forgettable talk from an unforgettable one? Not volume, and not vocabulary. It is emphasis that does the work — the art of placing one idea in the spotlight and holding it there until the audience cannot look away.

Our Grade 11 reading club noticed this while comparing Melville's Moby Dick with a handful of famous speeches. Captain Ahab is, above all, a rhetorician: he does not simply order his crew to hunt the whale — he persuades them. Mateo observed that Ahab repeats a single image again and again, so that what the sailors finally believe is the captain's obsession, not their own reason.

Great orators use the same trick. It was in the closing lines of the most celebrated speeches that history was made, precisely because the speaker narrowed everything down to one unforgettable claim. Nadia put it neatly: “What a crowd remembers is a feeling, rarely the exact words.”

For the Inspiring Nordic project, this matters enormously. Each of us is preparing a short persuasive piece, and Sofía reminded the club that a cluttered argument convinces nobody. The discipline of the cleft sentence — It is… that…, What… is… — forces us to decide what truly counts and to give it pride of place.

So before you write your next paragraph, ask the ruthless question the whale seems to ask Ahab: of everything you could say, what is the one thing that must not be missed? Answer that, put it in the spotlight, and let the rest fall quietly into the background.

data.title: Cleft sentences (It is… that… / What… is…)
data.intro: When we want to highlight one part of a sentence, we can split it in two — a 'cleft'. English has two common patterns: the it-cleft (It is X that…) and the wh-cleft (What… is X).

examples.text: It is the message that matters, not the volume.
What great speakers do is control our attention.
It was in 1863 that the speech was delivered.
What we remember is the feeling, not the words.

rules: Use It + is/was + the focus + that/who to spotlight a noun, phrase or adverbial: It was Sofía who spoke first.
Use What… + is/was + focus to highlight an action or idea: What matters is honesty.
Keep the tense consistent across the split: It is emphasis that counts; It was Liam who won.

items.sentence: ___ the message that matters, not the noise.
___ great writers do is cut every unnecessary word.
It was Liam ___ opened the debate.
___ we remember is the feeling, not the words.
It ___ in the final line that the point became clear.

data.script: Good morning, Grade 11. Today we study cleft sentences — the elegant way to put the spotlight on what matters. Think of a great speech: it is one idea that the speaker repeats until we remember it. What powerful writers do is control our attention. For our Inspiring Nordic project, each of you will polish one persuasive line. Liam will present first on Thursday. Remember: it is emphasis that turns a sentence into a message. Bring your boldest claim, and make every word count.

activities.title: Speaking — a persuasive appeal. In pairs, then record it.

data.text: In pairs, prepare a one-minute persuasive appeal for the Inspiring Nordic project, using at least one cleft sentence to spotlight your key idea. Model: “It is trust, not talent, that holds a team together.” 1) What single change would most improve your school? 2) Persuasion or honesty — which matters more in public speaking? 3) When does emphasis become manipulation? Give reasons and examples, then record your discussion.

homework.prompt: Write a short persuasive paragraph (10–12 sentences) about an idea worth defending, using at least three cleft sentences (It is… that…, What… is…, It was… who…) to place your key points in the spotlight. Capital letters and full stops!
